BMW M4 GT3.notes: Front-engine GT3. More stable on the brakes than mid/rear-engine cars. Can run slightly more rearward brake bias. Tends to understeer on entry.

Porsche 911 GT3 R (991.2).notes: Rear-engine. Natural rear weight bias gives great traction but can snap oversteer on lift-off. Needs more front downforce than most GT3s. Run stiffer front springs to compensate for rear weight.

Mercedes-AMG GT3.notes: Long wheelbase front-engine. Very stable platform, excellent on fast tracks. Can struggle to rotate in tight corners. Benefits from aggressive diff settings.

McLaren 720S GT3.notes: Mid-engine, well balanced. Good all-rounder. Slightly more aero-efficient than rivals. Can run slightly less wing for same downforce.

Ferrari 296 GT3.notes: V6 turbo mid-engine. Strong power delivery, good aero platform. Turbo lag at low RPM means smoother throttle maps help corner exit.

Audi R8 LMS GT3 Evo II.notes: Mid-engine V10 naturally aspirated. Linear power delivery, predictable handling. Slightly heavier than rivals. Good on brakes due to V10 engine braking.

Lamborghini Huracan GT3 EVO2.notes: Similar platform to Audi R8 GT3. Mid-engine V10. Slightly more aggressive aero. Good mechanical grip.

Aston Martin Vantage GT3.notes: Front-engine V8 turbo. Good straight-line speed, stable on brakes. Can struggle in very tight sections. Turbo delivery needs smooth inputs.

Porsche 911 RSR (2017).notes: Rear-engine GTE. Incredible rear traction, notorious for entry understeer. Needs aggressive front aero and soft front springs. Run minimum rear wing possible.

Ferrari 488 GTE.notes: Mid-engine turbo V8 GTE. Well balanced, strong in medium-speed corners. Turbo needs smooth throttle application.

Corvette C8.R.notes: Mid-engine flat-plane V8. Excellent power delivery, strong on the brakes. Good top speed. Slightly heavier than European rivals.

Oreca 07 LMP2.notes: The dominant LMP2 chassis. Very aero dependent — ride height is critical. Small changes to ride height have massive effects. No ABS, so brake modulation matters.

Dallara P217 LMP2.notes: Alternative LMP2 chassis. Slightly different aero characteristics to Oreca. More forgiving at the limit but slightly less peak downforce.

Dallara F3.notes: Formula 3 car. No driver aids. Great car to learn open-wheel racing. Aero matters a lot but power is moderate so traction is manageable.

Dallara IR-18 (IndyCar).notes: IndyCar. Massive power, big downforce. Very different road course vs oval setup. No aids at all — demands respect. Push-to-pass system means power spikes.

BMW 320 TC (WTCC).notes: Front-wheel drive touring car. Completely different driving style — trail braking rotates the car, throttle straightens it. Needs very different diff approach. Brake bias more rearward than RWD.

Chevrolet Cruze TC1 (WTCC).notes: Front-wheel drive touring car. Similar characteristics to BMW 320 TC. Slightly more power means more torque steer to manage.

Shelby Cobra 427.notes: Massive V8 in a tiny body. Brutal power-to-weight. Will kill you if you're not careful. Very soft suspension by modern standards. Needs smooth throttle and conservative diff. The rear WILL step out on you.

Ferrari 250 GTO.notes: Front-engine V12. More refined than the Cobra but still no aids. Better weight distribution. Drum brakes (if modeled) fade quickly. Beautiful to drive when you respect it.

Ford GT40 Mk I.notes: Mid-engine Le Mans winner. Better balanced than front-engine historics. Low roofline means poor visibility. Surprisingly good brakes for the era. Gearing is critical — original only had 4-speed.

Porsche 917K.notes: Rear-engine flat-12 monster. Terrifying power-to-weight. Early aero was sketchy — high-speed stability is the #1 concern. Legendary tail-happy handling. Short wheelbase + rear engine + 600hp = constant attention required.

Jaguar E-Type Lightweight.notes: Front-engine inline-6. Graceful and well balanced for its era. Long nose means weight is forward — good on brakes, can understeer mid-corner.

Lotus 49.notes: DFV-powered, no wings in original spec. One of the most dangerous cars ever built. The engine IS the chassis (stressed member). Zero aero grip, all mechanical. Will spin without warning. Needs very conservative setup.

Lotus 79.notes: First ground-effect F1 car. MASSIVE downforce from the underbody tunnels. Ride height is CRITICAL — too high and you lose all ground effect. Very planted until the aero stalls, then snap oversteer.

Brabham BT20.notes: 1960s F1 car. No wings, pure mechanical grip. Less powerful than the Lotus 49 but more forgiving. Good car to learn historic open-wheel racing.

March 701.notes: Early wings era F1 car. Some downforce but crude aero. Better than no-wing cars at high speed but still needs respect. Wings add some setup options.

Porsche 962C.notes: Turbo flat-6 Group C car. Ground effect + turbo power = very fast but demanding. Turbo lag is significant — need smooth throttle. Ride height critical for ground effect.

Jaguar XJR-9.notes: V12 Group C car. Massive naturally aspirated power — instant throttle response unlike turbo rivals. More predictable power delivery but still brutal.

Nissan R89C.notes: Twin-turbo V8 Group C car. Good aero platform. Turbo delivery needs management. Slightly heavier than Porsche but more stable.

Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 (NASCAR).notes: NASCAR Cup car. V8 pushrod engine. Heavy, powerful, crude. Setup is completely different for road course vs oval. On ovals: stagger (different tire sizes L/R) is key. On road courses: brake bias matters most.

Ford Mustang (NASCAR).notes: NASCAR Cup car. Similar to Camaro but slightly different aero profile. Marginally better top speed, slightly less downforce.

Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR (1955).notes: Inline-8 fuel-injected sports racer. Famously driven by Moss/Jenkinson at the Mille Miglia. Drum brakes with air scoops. Very fast for its era but no modern safety features. Inboard front brakes reduce unsprung weight.

Jaguar D-Type (1955).notes: Le Mans winning sports racer. Inline-6 with disc brakes — revolutionary for the era. Monocoque construction. The small fin on the headrest aids high-speed stability. Better braking than drum-brake rivals.

Aston Martin DBR1 (1959).notes: Inline-6, Le Mans winner 1959. Disc brakes all round. Relatively light. Good handling balance for the era. More refined than rivals. Lower power than Mercedes but better chassis.

Ferrari 250 Testa Rossa (1958).notes: V12 sports racer. Multiple Le Mans wins. Drum brakes (early), disc (later). Beautiful pontoon-fender body. High-revving V12 gives good engine braking. Relatively light but drums fade in endurance.

Ferrari 330 P4 (1967).notes: Mid-engine V12 sports prototype. One of the most beautiful race cars ever. Three-valve heads, Lucas fuel injection. Incredibly responsive engine. Mid-engine layout was revolutionary for Ferrari at the time.

Porsche 906 Carrera 6 (1966).notes: Lightweight flat-6 rear-engine sports car. Only 210hp but very light. Fiberglass body. Excellent handling due to low weight. The start of Porsche's legendary prototype lineage.

Porsche 910 (1967).notes: Evolution of the 906. Flat-6 or flat-8 engine options. Better aerodynamics and suspension than the 906. Light and nimble.

Lola T70 Mk III (1967).notes: Chevrolet V8 powered sports prototype. Massive power in a relatively light car. Popular in Can-Am and endurance racing. Big-block American V8 torque means careful throttle management needed. Sounds incredible.

Chaparral 2E (1966).notes: Pioneering high wing Can-Am car. First race car with a moveable aero device. Chevrolet V8. The wing was driver-adjustable — full angle in corners, flat on straights. Revolutionary for its time.

Ferrari 275 GTB/C (1966).notes: Competition version of the road-going 275 GTB. V12, rear transaxle. Better weight distribution than most front-engine cars of the era. Aluminum body panels save weight. A true gentleman racer's GT.

AC Cobra 289 (1963).notes: The smaller-engine Cobra. More balanced than the 427 big-block version. Ford 289 V8 is less explosive but more manageable. Better handling than the 427. Lighter and more nimble. Good introduction to Cobra racing.

Cooper T51 (1959).notes: First rear-engine F1 World Champion car. Coventry Climax engine. Small and nimble. Revolutionized F1 — proved rear-engine was the future. Modest power but excellent handling for its era.

Lotus 25 (1963).notes: First monocoque F1 car. Jim Clark's championship winner. Revolutionary lightweight construction. Climax V8 engine. Incredible cornering for its time due to low weight and good balance.

Ferrari 312 (1967).notes: Ferrari's V12 F1 car. More power than the DFV rivals but heavier. Beautiful engine note. Handles differently due to weight of the V12. Needs careful braking due to rear weight bias.

McLaren M23 (1974).notes: Emerson Fittipaldi and James Hunt's championship car. DFV-powered. One of the first F1 cars with significant wing development. Reliable and well-balanced. Good all-rounder for the era.

Tyrrell P34 (1976).notes: The six-wheeled F1 car! Four small front wheels for reduced frontal area. DFV-powered. Won the 1976 Swedish GP. Unique braking characteristics — four front tires = massive front braking capacity. Higher brake bias than normal.

Ferrari 312T (1975).notes: Niki Lauda's championship car. Flat-12 engine, transverse gearbox. The flat-12 gave a lower center of gravity than the DFV V8. Excellent mechanical grip. The 'T' stands for transverse gearbox.

Williams FW07 (1979).notes: Ground-effect Williams. Alan Jones' championship car. DFV-powered. Excellent ground-effect design by Patrick Head. Ride height critical — too high loses downforce completely. Very fast when it works.

Porsche 935 (1977).notes: Turbo flat-6 Group 5 911 derivative. 'Moby Dick' variant had slant-nose body. Massive turbo lag then explosive power delivery. One of the most successful customer race cars ever. Rear-engine + turbo = very challenging.

Porsche 934 (1976).notes: Group 4 turbo 911. Closer to road car than the 935. Turbo lag is significant. Heavier than the 935. More accessible but still demands respect with that rear engine + turbo combo.

BMW 3.0 CSL (1975).notes: The 'Batmobile' with its wild aero kit. Inline-6 front-engine. Large rear wing and front splitter for the era. Dominated European touring car racing. Relatively well-balanced front-engine car. Good brakes.

De Tomaso Pantera Group 4 (1972).notes: Italian chassis with Ford Cleveland V8. Mid-engine, huge power. Raced extensively in Group 4. Massive torque from the American V8. Better balanced than front-engine muscle but brutal on throttle.

Porsche 956 (1982).notes: The original Group C ground-effect Porsche. Twin-turbo flat-6. Aluminum monocoque. Won Le Mans 1982-85. Ground effect is massive — ride height is the single most important setup parameter. Predecessor to the 962. Turbo lag requires smooth inputs.

Lancia LC2 (1983).notes: Ferrari V8 twin-turbo in a Lancia chassis. Incredibly powerful but unreliable. More power than the Porsche 956 but less developed aero. Challenging to drive — the power can overwhelm the grip.

Sauber-Mercedes C9 (1989).notes: Mercedes-Benz twin-turbo V8 Group C car. Dominant in 1989, won Le Mans. More refined than earlier Group C cars. Better aero development. Silver color revived the Silver Arrows heritage.

Mazda 787B (1991).notes: 4-rotor Wankel rotary engine. Won Le Mans 1991 — the only rotary winner. Legendary exhaust note. Engine revs very freely. Light weight. The rotary's linear power delivery is actually easier to manage than turbo rivals.

Toyota 88C-V (1988).notes: Toyota's Group C contender. V8 twin-turbo. Strong but never quite beat the Porsches at Le Mans. Good chassis, reliable. Developed into later Le Mans cars.

Ford Sierra RS500 Cosworth (1987).notes: Turbo 4-cylinder Group A touring car. Dominated BTCC and Bathurst 1000. Huge turbo power in a relatively light package. Rear-wheel drive with turbo lag makes it a real handful. The whale-tail rear wing is iconic.

BMW M3 E30 Group A (1987).notes: Naturally aspirated inline-4 Group A. Dominated DTM and touring car racing globally. Less power than the turbo Sierra but more driveable and consistent. High-revving engine — keep it in the powerband. Beautiful handling.

Mercedes 190E 2.5-16 Evo II (1992).notes: DTM-spec Mercedes. Cosworth-developed 2.5L inline-4. The aggressive body kit was functional aero. Rear-wheel drive, no aids. Competitive with the M3 in DTM. Slightly more power, slightly heavier.

Alfa Romeo 155 V6 TI (1993).notes: V6 DTM car that was controversially classified as FWD (debated — had rear drive too). Dominated 1993 DTM. If modeled as FWD: trail-brake rotation technique essential. Very quick but handling polarizes opinion.

Nissan Skyline GT-R R32 Group A (1990).notes: Godzilla. Twin-turbo RB26 inline-6 with ATTESA all-wheel-drive. Dominated Japanese touring car racing so thoroughly it was banned. AWD gives incredible traction but the car is heavy. Turbo lag is present.

Williams FW14B (1992).notes: Nigel Mansell's dominant championship car. Renault V10. Active suspension, traction control, semi-auto gearbox. One of the most technologically advanced F1 cars ever. If modeled with active suspension, ride height is less critical. Incredibly fast.

McLaren MP4/4 (1988).notes: Most dominant F1 car ever — won 15 of 16 races. Honda turbo V6. Senna and Prost. Last year of turbo era. Incredible power but turbo lag in qualifying trim. Beautiful Gordon Murray design.

Lotus 98T (1986).notes: Renault turbo V6 with over 1000hp in qualifying trim. Ayrton Senna's car. Insane power-to-weight. The turbo lag then sudden power delivery is lethal. No traction aids. Arguably the scariest F1 car to drive.

Ferrari 640 (1989).notes: First F1 car with a semi-automatic gearbox. V12 engine. Beautiful John Barnard design. Nigel Mansell won on debut at Brazil. The V12 gives incredible throttle response and engine braking.

Brabham BT52 (1983).notes: Nelson Piquet's championship car. BMW turbo inline-4. Arrow-shaped design by Gordon Murray. The turbo could produce massive boost in qualifying. Pioneered refuelling pit stops to run lighter.

McLaren F1 GTR (1995).notes: BMW V12 mid-engine. Won Le Mans 1995. Road car converted to racer. Central driving position (in road spec). Naturally aspirated so linear power. Carbon fiber construction. One of the greatest GT cars ever built. The 'long tail' version has more downforce.

Porsche 911 GT1 (1998).notes: Mid-engine turbo flat-6 homologation special. Won Le Mans 1998. Despite the 911 name, it's essentially a prototype with 911 headlights. Twin-turbo needs smooth throttle. Very high downforce for a 'GT' car.

Mercedes CLK-GTR (1997).notes: V12 GT1 homologation car. Won 1997 FIA GT championship. Front-mid engine layout. Imposing and fast. The Mercedes had the most power of the GT1 cars.

Toyota GT-One TS020 (1998).notes: Twin-turbo V8 Le Mans car. Incredibly fast — led Le Mans but never won. Massive downforce, very aero-dependent. Ride height critical. One of the fastest GT1-era cars. Had traction control.

Nissan R390 GT1 (1998).notes: Twin-turbo V8 GT1 car based on a Tom Walkinshaw design. Finished 3rd at Le Mans 1998. Reliable but not quite fast enough. Distinctive Japanese styling. Good all-rounder.

BMW V12 LMR (1999).notes: V12 Le Mans winner 1999. Open-top prototype. Williams-designed aero. Naturally aspirated V12 — linear power delivery. TC available. Clean aero design. Won in unusual circumstances (Mercedes flip).
